headline: Buyers of $22 Billion Bank Securities Are Trapped in Losing Bet
author: Tasos Vossos

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A $22 billion group of US bank preferred shares has been slumping harder than even the riskiest junk bonds this year — and investors have no good way out of the trade.

Some fixed-for-life preferred shares sold by banks during the pandemic era have lost 8.5% in total return terms this year, making the group one of the worst-performing parts of the global credit market. The securities have plummeted nearly 40% since they were sold and every issuer so far has skipped repayment options that would have been investors' way out without a loss. A pending decision by Morgan Stanley may make it a clean sweep.

Unlike other types of preferred shares, fixed-for-life coupons never change, making them extremely sensitive to interest rates. Now, with rates significantly higher than in 2020 and 2021, when lenders sold the securities with sub-5% coupons, the banks have no incentive to replace them.
That's left investors, who were attracted by their relatively high yields at the time, effectively trapped in a losing bet.

"Would you buy 100-year bonds? No? Well, that's what you're buying," said Frank Sileo, senior fixed income strategist Americas at the UBS Chief Investment Office. "These are truly perpetual preferreds."

The losses for this group of preferreds are outsized even in a fixed income market that has come under intense pressure this year. Government bond yields have been rising on the back of inflation and public spending concerns, while the lowest-rated junk bonds are coming under strain.

The selloff has left the pandemic-era securities trading at deeply discounted levels. The group is indicated at a price of 61 cents on the dollar on average, based on data compiled by Bloomberg. Among the issuers are major banks like JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Wells Fargo & Co., which have already skipped call options.

Morgan Stanley's $1.3 billion issue, which has a call option in January, is indicated at 61.4 cents on the dollar, implying virtually no chance of early repayment. A representative for Morgan Stanley declined to comment.
Preferreds are a type of hybrid security similar to Europe's Additional Tier 1 bonds, and are popular with US banks because they help meet capital requirements without diluting common shareholders.

The fixed-for-life flavor — also known for their retail investor-friendly par amount of $25 — proliferated when interest rates were slashed during the pandemic. Banks seized the opportunity to lock in cheap capital, with lenders selling about $10 billion of the securities in 2020 and $16 billion in 2021.

"Some banks had the foresight that rates might not always be zero forever. Given demand for those instruments, why not issue some fixed-for-life," said Arnold Kakuda, senior financials credit analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.

For buyers of fixed-for-life preferreds, coupons that were multiple times the Treasury yield seemed generous at a time when yields on all bonds had collapsed. And their bet may have worked out if rates had stayed lower for longer.

But now, the fixed coupons on these securities — many of which are below 5% — look far too low. The lowest-coupon issue in the group, a 3.75% series by US Bancorp, is now indicated at 55 cents on the dollar.

By contrast, fixed-for-life bank preferreds sold in 2026 have carried coupons of 6.69% on average, though this type of preferred shares has fallen out of favor. Banks are now issuing more fixed-to-reset preferreds, where the coupon switches to a market-based level after a certain period.

To be sure, "when we talk about perpetuity, anything can happen," said BI's Kakuda. "Never say never. Who would have thought negative rates would be possible but it happened," he said, referring to the potential for the securities to rebound in price and be repaid in the future.

Still, it's highly unlikely that rates will move in favor of the preferred-share investors anytime soon. If anything, Treasury yields rose back toward 5% this week after new evidence of sticky inflation boosted the odds of interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve.

At the same time, regulatory requirements prevent banks from adding any clauses to preferred shares that would give an incentive to call them, meaning the decision is purely based on whether it is economic for the lender to do so.
This points to an extended period of pain for holders of fixed-for-life preferred shares, and no way out apart from selling at deeply depressed levels.
"The seeds of dramatic losses were sown in 2020 and 2021," said UBS's Sileo. "I was talking about it at the time. What's going to happen when the music ends?"
